Juvenile Strongylocentrotus droebachiensis undergo a dramatic transformation during the planktotrophic larval phase, culminating in metamorphosis and settlement. Under laboratory conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the time since birth at metamorphosis has been documented at approximately 45 days , a period that reflects the duration required for the bipinnaria larva to develop the adult rudiment and achieve metamorphic competence. Newly settled individuals then enter the post-metamorphic juvenile stage, characterized by rapid test growth and the commencement of grazing on benthic microalgae. The initial wet weight at birth, representing the mass of the fertilized ovum, is remarkably low, estimated at approximately 0.000000268 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000000268 grams]. This minute starting mass highlights the extreme energetic demands placed on the developing pluteus larva, which must rely entirely on exogenous phytoplankton grazing from the onset of the exotrophic transition.

Sexual maturation in the green sea urchin involves a pronounced shift in somatic investment toward reproductive tissue. The test diameter at puberty, marking the onset of gametogenesis, has been determined to be 2.175 centimeters [Lp = 2.175 centimeters], a size at which individuals begin to allocate resources toward gonad development. This threshold is significantly smaller than the ultimate test diameter, which for this species reaches 8.7 centimeters [Li = 8.7 centimeters] in large, reproductively active adults. Correspondingly, the wet weight at puberty is calculated to be 4.78 grams [Wwp = 4.78 grams], representing a substantial increase from the hatchling mass but still far below the mature adult size. Individuals at this stage exhibit the first signs of reproductive activation, though they may not achieve full reproductive output until reaching a larger body size and more favorable environmental conditions.

Body size at the population level is characterized by substantial variation, with the largest adults approaching a remarkable asymptotic mass. The ultimate wet weight for Strongylocentrotus droebachiensis has been recorded at 306 grams [Wwi = 306 grams], a value consistent with the species' status as one of the larger echinoids in the North Atlantic. This maximum body mass is achieved through years of continuous growth, with individuals gradually increasing both test diameter and soft tissue mass. In comparison, the wet weight at puberty of 4.78 grams represents only a small fraction of this ultimate size, underscoring the protracted nature of somatic growth before reproductive maturity. Field surveys in the Gulf of Maine indicate that urchins of this maximum size are typically found in deeper, cooler waters where predation pressure is lower and food resources are more predictable. The gonadal tissue of these large adults constitutes a significant portion of their total body mass.

At a water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) has been measured at 21% [GSI = 21%]. This relatively high index suggests that Strongylocentrotus droebachiensis invests heavily in gamete production during the spawning season, a strategy common among echinoids that rely on broadcast fertilisation. The index also exhibits pronounced seasonal variation, typically peaking in late winter or early spring when phytoplankton blooms trigger the release of gametes. Laboratory experiments have shown that individuals maintained at constant 12 °C with ad libitum feeding can sustain elevated GSI values for extended periods, indicating that temperature rather than food limitation is the primary regulator of gonadal development in this species.

Longevity estimates for this sea urchin suggest a comparatively extended lifespan relative to many other echinoderms. At a rearing temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the maximum documented lifespan is approximately 16 years [am = approximately 16 years]. This considerable longevity, inferred from mark-recapture studies and size-frequency analyses of populations in the northwestern Atlantic, allows individuals to accumulate substantial body mass over time and to participate in multiple spawning seasons. The slow pace of growth and late onset of reproductive maturity are balanced by this extended adult lifespan, which provides numerous opportunities for successful reproduction. Mortality rates in natural populations are highest among recently metamorphosed juveniles and decrease steadily as individuals reach larger test diameters and stronger defensive spines.
